q-216200.name: Question 1
q-216200.worked_solution:
Since parallel lines have equal slopes, both lines should have the same slope.

First, let's find the slope of the line passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(3,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{-1-1}{3-2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{1} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we wish to find a line that has a slope of $-2$ and passes through the point $(0,2).$ To find the equation of this line, we use the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =-2(x-0) \\ y-2 & =-2x \\ y & =-2x+2\end{aligned}
$$

q-216203.name: Question 2
q-216203.worked_solution:
Since parallel lines have equal slopes, both lines should have the same slope.

First, let's find the slope of the line passing through the points $(1,-1)$ and $(2,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{5-(-1)}{2-1} \\  & =\frac{5+1}{2-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{1} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we wish to find a line that has a slope of $6$ and passes through the point $(0,3).$ To find the equation of this line, we use the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =6(x-0) \\ y-3 & =6x \\ y & =6x+3\end{aligned}
$$

q-216212.name: Question 3
q-216212.worked_solution:
Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line $3x+y=1.$ 

To find the slope of the line $3x+y=1,$ we convert the equation to slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+y & =1 \\ y & =-3x+1\end{aligned}
$$

From the slope-intercept form, we can tell that the slope of the line is $-3.$

So, we want a line with the slope $-3$ that passes through the point $(1,1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-3(x-1) \\ y-1 & =-3x+3 \\ y & =-3x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write this equation in standard form.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-3x+4 \\ 3x+y & =4\end{aligned}
$$
